title: Reporters on the Job: From Toronto to Nairobi
text:
Reporters on the Job: From Toronto to Nairobi
Every week, a selection of Monitor staffers and contributors share their challenges and insights from reporting around the globe.
Toronto – Sara Miller Llana
One of the best parts of being a reporter is getting to access places, people, and events you’d never experience in ordinary life. But sometimes it works in reverse – your life offers the perfect anecdote for a story. That’s what happened with an August piece on the rise of women’s basketball. A friend in Toronto had invited me to see the Toronto Tempo play. A few days later, I was sitting in on a features meeting when I heard staff writer Kendra Nordin Beato pitch a story about the WNBA, including the culture-war debates swirling around the Indiana Fever. “Wait,” I said. “I’m going to see the Tempo play the Fever!” And that’s how a night out with a new friend turned into a reporting assignment, and eventually the lede of Kendra’s story.
Chelmsford, Massachusetts – Cameron Pugh
Reporters rarely work alone. At the Monitor, every word I write gets backstopped by whip-smart editors and a diligent copydesk. I regularly run ideas by my fellow reporters, too. But beyond my colleagues, I often rely most on the people I interview to help me understand the stories I’m trying to tell. A recent story on immigration court had me wading into a complicated, poorly understood government system. Reporting in a disorderly courtroom, I felt as if I was barely treading water. But I was accompanied by Michele Cantara, a dedicated volunteer who has spent more than a year watching immigration proceedings. Her astute explanations, along with conversations with former immigration judges and other experts, helped turn a convoluted topic into a clear story. 
Ceuta, Spain – Colette Davidson
Reporting in a foreign country carries uncertainty: Will I be able to communicate? Will I find enough sources? How lost will I get? Rarely do I worry about whether I’ll make it to my destination in one piece. But as I sat strapped in next to 14 strangers in my first-ever helicopter ride to Ceuta – an autonomous Spanish city on the northern coast of Africa, bordering Morocco – part of me wondered. As my fellow passengers chatted nonchalantly about the weather, I closed my eyes and gripped my purse while we chugged over the Strait of Gibraltar. Once we touched down and I got to work reporting on the migration crisis here, I felt ready to handle anything.
Nairobi, Kenya – Sophie Neiman
Rows of dusty wooden boxes line the walls of Steve Collins’ butterfly archive. There are about 1 million butterflies on these shelves, and another 3 million pinned in storage in the back. I rush to note as many specimens as possible, pen bleeding through the paper of my reporter’s journal. It is too big to comprehend. But this, I think, is the perfect metaphor for the job of a journalist: to make sense of the overwhelming. I begin by asking Mr. Collins what each butterfly means to him. That personal connection is a way to understand his vast collection. We retire to his veranda, where he begins to tell his life story.
